extracted.intended_audience: psychologists, physiologists, and observers of infant development (researchers and informed parents)
extracted.subtask_description: Methodical, longitudinal observation and recording of newborn infants' sensations, movements, and speech to trace the psychogenesis of will, intellect, feelings, and language. Emphasizes multiple independent observers, daily record-keeping, sensory and motor tests, and attention to timing of developmental milestones.

rubrics_metrics.name: Begin with methodical investigation of the child
rubrics_metrics.description: Whoever would watch the growth of the human mind must first make the soul of the child the object of a methodical investigation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Study infants directly rather than relying on secondhand volumes; approach observation systematically and scientifically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Start the study with sensations and movements
rubrics_metrics.description: The study must begin with the observation of the sensations and movements of the child.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: No mental activity without sensation; observe how sensation and movement interact as the basis for will and later intellect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer multiple independent observers and comparisons
rubrics_metrics.description: A number of men well versed in physiology should, independently of each other, carefully observe as many infants as possible, and compare results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Independent replication and inter-observer comparison are necessary to build reliable knowledge; avoid single-observer anecdote bias.

rubrics_metrics.name: Encourage exchange of observations among parents/friends
rubrics_metrics.description: Fathers of children, friends to each other, should mutually exchange observations upon their own children.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pooling domestic longitudinal data complements professional observations and increases sample variety.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep a daily day-book from birth
rubrics_metrics.description: Individuals should keep a day-book of the acts of their children from their birth upward.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Record daily occurrences; the author notes that in the first two years 'hardly a day passes ... in which something does not occur worthy of notice.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish reflexive from voluntary actions
rubrics_metrics.description: Differentiate reflex movements (e.g., early cries, palmar grasp) from intentional voluntary actions as the will develops.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use repeated observation and specific tests (e.g., placing finger in palm, presenting objects) to determine whether a response is reflexive or purposeful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Observe the reciprocal action of sensation and movement leading to will
rubrics_metrics.description: The reciprocal action of sensation and movement leads to the beginning of development of the will; as the will becomes effective the intellect reveals itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Track how sensory experiences and motor activity progressively enable intentional actions, speech, and feelings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attribute earliest uncoordinated movements to inherited motor energy
rubrics_metrics.description: Early aimless movements are due to inherited discharge of surplus motive energy from motor organs before restraint by the brain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider inherited physiological explanations for early motor patterns rather than assuming imitation or purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Document motor milestone timing (head, sitting, standing, walking)
rubrics_metrics.description: Record when the child first shows voluntary head-holding, sitting, standing, and walking (author notes holding head ~14 weeks, sitting ~10 months, standing end of first year, walking thereafter).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observe whether acquisitions come suddenly or gradually; note effects of supports and preceding unsuccessful attempts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Observe development and transitions in grasping
rubrics_metrics.description: Track progression from reflexive palmar grasp in first quarter-year to first intentional reaching (~seventeenth week) and subsequent refinement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Note thumb participation, bringing objects to mouth and eyes, pleasure and wonder at grasping, and whether progress is abrupt or slow.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monitor emergence of social reaching and attachment
rubrics_metrics.description: Watch for transition from grasping indifferent objects to reaching for parents (noted toward end of fourth month) as a sign of social/affective development.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use reaching and arm-raising toward caregivers as evidence of developing recognition and attachment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Study multisensory integration when objects are explored
rubrics_metrics.description: When sight, touch, smell, and taste are combined at a single object, this junction excites surprise, induces reflection, and arouses inquiry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Present objects that afford combinations (color, texture, weight, temperature, smell, taste) and record exploratory behaviors (rubbing, mouthing, disassembly).

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess tactile sensitivity and its early low level
rubrics_metrics.description: New-born skin sensibility is very low; reflex cries are not expressions of pain; sensibility to temperature and touch increases within days.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carefully observe responses to touch and to potentially painful stimuli, recognizing that absence of outward distress does not necessarily indicate absence of injury.

rubrics_metrics.name: Test taste discrimination from birth
rubrics_metrics.description: All new-born children could distinguish strong tastes; sugar produces a satisfied reaction while quinine, vinegar, salt produce distaste.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use controlled taste applications to determine preferences and note that taste is among the first senses giving clear perceptions and supporting memory/judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examine early olfactory discrimination
rubrics_metrics.description: Infants appear able to distinguish odors very early and can recognize different foods or nurses by scent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observe aversions or preferences to odors (e.g., tobacco smoke unpleasant, camphor pleasant) and note role of smell in guiding feeding behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate auditory development and early deafness at birth
rubrics_metrics.description: All infants are functionally deaf at birth due to closed outer ear; responses to strong sounds appear within hours to days (earliest ~6 hours).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess response to strong sounds (startle, body movement, blinking); failure to respond after ear is suitable for hearing is a sign of deafness; hearing is crucial for early intellectual development.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use sound (voices, songs, music) as diagnostic and soothing stimuli
rubrics_metrics.description: Voices of mother and relatives are earliest impressions; cradle songs soothe while dance-music can excite; certain consonant sounds quiet children while novel loud noises may provoke crying.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observe differential effects of specific sounds and tones to characterize auditory discrimination and affective responses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Track visual development and eye coordination
rubrics_metrics.description: Vision begins with light/dark discrimination; early eye movements are unregulated (no symmetry first six days); staring begins ~9 days; following moving objects rarely before three weeks; accommodation and binocular coordination develop over months.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Test light sensitivity, tracking moving objects, binocular coordination, accommodation, and the gradual emergence of a steady, intelligent gaze.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess color, form, distance, and magnitude perception progression
rubrics_metrics.description: Color preferences appear early (yellow/red disliked black/dazzling lights); fine color naming often not before third year; recognition of forms and distance estimation proceed slowly and often require tactile confirmation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design experiments for color preference, form recognition (touch + sight), and distance/magnitude estimation; expect large individual variability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differentiate inherited reflexes from acquired habits
rubrics_metrics.description: Some reactions (pupil contraction to light) are inherited; others (blinking to threats) are acquired and become habitual by repetition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use repeated exposures and developmental timing to determine whether a response is innate reflex or learned protective habit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Collect large amount of material before generalizing
rubrics_metrics.description: We have an array of facts with little connection; much material must be collected before clearly setting forth the sensual basis of spiritual growth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasize extensive data collection across individuals and contexts before drawing broad theoretical conclusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep daily written records of all speech-like utterances
rubrics_metrics.description: Set down daily on paper every expression, every sound that could be represented in writing, uttered by a child during the first two years.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Systematic transcription of sounds provides a basis for reconstructing the history of speech development and for later publication/analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for imitation when studying speech acquisition
rubrics_metrics.description: It is hard to exclude imitation from the child; separate what is acquired by imitation from what is inherited — speech predisposition is inherited though not fully formed at birth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design observations/controls that consider both inherited predispositions and environmental imitation influences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Document phonetic/phoneme emergence and babbling timeline
rubrics_metrics.description: Vowel-sounds appear first; consonant 'm' may appear ~7 weeks; by seventh month m, b, d, n, r (rare g, h; very rarely k) are observable; syllables pa, ta, ma, etc., are common.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Record precise timing of specific phonemes and syllables, note when vocalizations begin to signify desires, and trace transition from reflexive sounds to meaningful utterances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classify cry types and correlate with internal states
rubrics_metrics.description: Different cries correspond to conditions: periodically broken cry with knit eyes = hunger; continuous whine = cold; high penetrating tone = pain; laughter/crow = pleasure; other gestures accompany desires.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Map cry acoustics and accompanying gestures to physiological/emotional states through repeated, contextualized observation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use experimental manipulations to elicit and observe responses
rubrics_metrics.description: Perform simple experiments (presenting/removing objects, applying tastes, making sounds, touching) to observe sensory, motor, and affective responses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Repeated controlled manipulations reveal developmental capacities (e.g., response to taste, smell, sound, light) and should be recorded longitudinally.
